titre: Thermopylae (480 BCE): There Were Not Three Hundred of Them
accroche: On the last day at Thermopylae, fourteen hundred Greeks were still holding the position alongside Leonidas's three hundred Spartans.
contenu_vulgarise:
In August 480 BCE, King Leonidas of Sparta holds the pass of Thermopylae, in central Greece, against the army of the Persian Great King Xerxes I. The Greek army gathered there does not number three hundred men: the historian Herodotus, the closest surviving source to the event, counts about seven thousand fighters from more than a dozen city-states, Spartans, but also Thespians, Thebans, Corinthians, Arcadians, Phocians and many others.

## Three Hundred, Then No One: What Herodotus Really Says

Leonidas's three hundred form a very real body: they are the hippeis, the king's three hundred personal guards, chosen from among the Spartans who already have a son to carry on their line. But they never fight alone. For two days, the narrow pass holds thanks to the whole Greek coalition. It is only on the third day, when a local, Ephialtes, reveals to the Persians a mountain path allowing them to bypass the position, that Leonidas sends away most of his army, keeping with him his three hundred Spartans, about seven hundred Thespian volunteers determined to stay, and a Theban contingent of four hundred men whom the sources say were held back by force. Spartans and Thespians fight to the last man; the Thebans, for their part, surrender before the final assault, and only a few are killed before their surrender is accepted. In all, at least a thousand men die on this last day, not three hundred.

Facing them, Herodotus gives the unverifiable and manifestly exaggerated figure of 2.6 million Persian fighters, support personnel included. Modern historians, cross-checking the logistical capacities of the time, settle instead on a range of 70,000 to 300,000 men: an order of magnitude far lower, but one that still leaves the Greeks at an overwhelming numerical disadvantage.

## Why “the Three Hundred” Erased the Others

The round, heroic number took hold in collective memory at the expense of the rest of the coalition: including the seven hundred Thespians, who made exactly the same choice as the Spartans and lost their lives there in even greater numbers. Herodotus himself does not tell a story of three hundred men abandoned to their fate: he tells that of a coalition of Greek city-states, whose volunteer rear guard numbered a thousand fighters. The legend simplified itself in the direction that best serves the story Sparta built after the fact about its own sacrifice: a phenomenon found, on other scales, whenever a battle becomes a symbol before remaining an event.

repere.texte: On the last day at Thermopylae, fourteen hundred Greeks are still holding the position alongside Leonidas (three hundred Spartans, seven hundred Thespians and four hundred Thebans), but the Thebans surrender before the final assault: it is the Spartans and Thespians, a thousand men, who die to the last man.
repere.source: Herodotus, *Histories*, VII, 222-225, as summarized by Wikipedia, “Battle of Thermopylae”

carte.punch: On the last day at Thermopylae, a thousand men die alongside Leonidas, not three hundred.
carte.idee: Herodotus describes a Greek coalition of seven thousand men. On the last day, Leonidas keeps three hundred Spartans, seven hundred Thespians and four hundred Thebans: the latter surrender before the end. Spartans and Thespians die to the last man: a thousand men, not three hundred.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full text of the book in which Herodotus details the Greek contingents engaged at Thermopylae.

quiz.question: Why did the figure of “three hundred” stay in collective memory, when Herodotus describes a much larger coalition at Thermopylae?
choix: Because the other Greek contingents deserted before the battle
Because Herodotus documented only the Spartans in his account
Because the archives of the other Greek city-states have all disappeared
Because the story simplified itself around the most heroic symbol
quiz.explication: Herodotus describes a coalition of about seven thousand men, then a final rear guard of fourteen hundred fighters (Spartans, Thespians and Thebans), of whom a thousand fight to the death, the Thebans having surrendered before the final assault.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Herodotus, how many Greek fighters, from more than a dozen city-states, initially gather at Thermopylae?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Herodotus, the source closest to the event, counts about seven thousand fighters from more than a dozen Greek city-states, not just the three hundred Spartans.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who reveals to the Persians the mountain path allowing them to bypass the Greek position at Thermopylae?
choix: A Spartan deserter trying to save his life
A Persian spy infiltrated into the Greek army
Leonidas himself, to spare the rest of his army
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Ephialtes, a local, who reveals to the Persians the mountain path allowing them to bypass the position, which prompts Leonidas to send away most of his army.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the four hundred Thebans of the rear guard do at the moment of the final assault?
choix: They surrender before the assault, and only a few are killed before their surrender is accepted
They fight to the last man, alongside the Spartans
They desert the night before, even before the Persians arrive
They join the Persian forces and turn their weapons against the Greeks
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Unlike the Spartans and Thespians, who fight to the last man, the Thebans surrender before the final assault, and only a few are killed before their surrender is accepted.
